# 2 Kings Chapter 24 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 244v–245r

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant for three years. Then he turned and rebelled against him.

**2** The LORD sent against him bands of Chaldeans, bands of Arameans, bands of Moabites, and bands of Ammonites. He sent them against Judah to destroy it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke through his servants the prophets.

**3** Surely this came upon Judah at the command of the LORD, to remove them from his presence, because of the sins of Manasseh, according to all that he had done,

**4** and also for the innocent blood that he had shed, for he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD was not willing to forgive.

**5** Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

**6** So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place.

**7** The king of Egypt did not come out of his land again, for the king of Babylon had taken all that belonged to the king of Egypt, from the Brook of Egypt to the river Euphrates.

**8** Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Nehushta daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem.

**9** He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father had done.

**10** At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up to Jerusalem, and the city was besieged.

**11** Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to the city while his servants were besieging it.

**12** Jehoiachin king of Judah surrendered to the king of Babylon — he, his mother, his servants, his officers, and his officials. The king of Babylon took him prisoner in the eighth year of his reign.

**13** He carried off all the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house, and cut in pieces all the vessels of gold in the temple of the LORD that Solomon king of Israel had made, as the LORD had foretold.

**14** He carried away all Jerusalem — all the officials, all the mighty warriors, ten thousand captives, and all the craftsmen and the smiths. None remained except the poorest people of the land.

**15** He carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon, along with the king's mother, the king's wives, his officials, and the leading men of the land. He took them into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon.

**16** All the men of valor, seven thousand, the craftsmen and the smiths, one thousand — all of them strong and fit for war — the king of Babylon brought captive to Babylon.

**17** The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place, and changed his name to Zedekiah.

**18** Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.

**19** He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.

**20** For because of the anger of the LORD it came to the point in Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Chapter 24 narrates the beginning of the end. The theological framework is relentless: verses 2-4 state explicitly that the destruction of Judah is YHWH's doing, in fulfillment of prophetic warnings, because of Manasseh's sins and especially his shedding of innocent blood. The statement that "the LORD was not willing to forgive" (v.4) is the Deuteronomistic history's most severe theological claim. The first deportation (597 BCE) strips Judah of its elite — military, artisan, and administrative classes — leaving only the poorest. Zedekiah's installation as puppet king and subsequent rebellion (v.20) sets the stage for the final catastrophe. The narrator's note that Egypt "did not come out of his land again" (v.7) closes off any hope of external rescue.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.1 — "came up" vs. "invaded the land"
- **EMET/LOGOS:** "came up"
- **PNEUMA:** "invaded the land"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "came up" — the Hebrew *'alah* (went up) is the standard verb for military advance toward Jerusalem. "Invaded" adds interpretive force not present in the text.

### V.6 — "slept with his fathers" vs. "died"
- **EMET/LOGOS:** "slept with his fathers"
- **PNEUMA:** "died"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "slept with his fathers" — the Hebrew idiom *vayishkav 'im avotayv* is the standard death formula and should be preserved as a recognizable pattern across Kings.

### V.12 — "gave himself up" vs. "surrendered"
- **EMET:** "went out to"
- **LOGOS:** "gave himself up"
- **PNEUMA:** "surrendered"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "surrendered" — the Hebrew *yatsa 'el* (went out to) in this military context clearly means surrender. "Surrendered" communicates the meaning directly without the excessive formality of "gave himself up."

### V.14 — "mighty warriors" vs. "soldiers"
- **EMET/LOGOS:** "mighty warriors"
- **PNEUMA:** "soldiers"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "mighty warriors" — *gibborey ha-chayil* is a specific term for elite fighting men, not generic soldiers.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
